newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil gov't takes on foes of civil service reform.
newsitem.headline: Brazil gov't takes on foes of civil service reform.

text.p: The Brazilian government on Thursday said it would spend the next two weeks fighting resistance in Congress to its civil service reform bill, after abandoning a first attempt to win approval of the legislation the previous day.
President Fernando Henrique Cardoso took advantage of a Thursday meeting with state governors to ask for their support in convincing lawmakers of the need to approve the proposed reforms.
"The president asked the governors to get involved to make sure the amendment is approved April 2," Benito Gama, the government's chief whip in the lower house, told reporters.
Other influential political figures, including Communications Minister Sergio Motta, would be enlisted to drum up support for the reform, officials said.

Civil service reform represents a powerful tool in the government's struggle to reduce public spending. But its main points -- an end to job guarantees for civil servants and a pay cap -- have met stiff resistance in Congress.

Last year, a key clause in the legislation was watered down, allowing only states and municipalities that spend more than 60 percent of revenues on payrolls to dismiss workers with so-called lifetime employment guarantees, and only after workers without such "stability" had been let go.

The main bone of contention now is the pay cap, which threatens to cut the income of lawmakers themselves. On Wednesday, opposition to that provision was largely responsible for stopping the first of two votes in the Chamber of Deputies on the reform, which takes the form of a constitutional amendment.

Many deputies and senators earn pensions from previous public sector posts on top of their monthly salaries of 8,000 reais ($7,620), taking them over the proposed monthly ceiling of 10,800 reais ($10,285) on pay and benefits.

The reform is also opposed by many judges, who fear local governments would use pay ceilings to pressure the judiciary. In addition, construction companies object to proposed new rules for public sector contracting. Powerful civil service trade unions also oppose the reform.
"Doing away with perks and benefits is never going to be easy in a democracy," said Deputy Wellington Moreira Franco, who has spent the last 19 months drawing up the legislation.
"It's not just the Chamber of Deputies that is against the reform -- it's the whole civil service," he said.
Talks between political party leaders and ministers to resolve the impasse were due to resume next week.

"Until a practical solution is found to the ceiling issue, the government won't put the reform to a vote because the whole bill could be undermined by one item," said a congressional official close to the negotiations.

One proposal, opposed by Moreira Franco but backed by Administration Minister Luiz Carlos Bresser, is to create a higher "super-ceiling" on pay and pensions for doctors, lawyers and other public sector professionals, including lawmakers.
Another option is to phase in the ceiling over a period of years, exempting the current Congress from its restrictions.
